event_info.event_description: Analyze for disclosures on global pandemic risks. Look for corporate language discussing widespread impacts like supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, remote work transitions, and fundamental shifts in consumer demand.

holistic_analysis: KMB’s 2024 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to material, still-unfolding business risks.  Although the initial outbreak is now roughly four years old, management describes continuing and forward-looking exposures: demand volatility, supply-chain and labor disruptions, cost inflation, remote-work cyber-vulnerabilities and shifts in consumer purchasing power.  The disclosures oscillate between historical impact (e.g., earlier supply-chain shocks) and present-day headwinds (elevated input costs expected to persist through 2024).  There are few hard numbers, but the narrative is detailed and specific, signalling a meaningful residual risk rather than a mere historical footnote.  Applying the Time-Decay Principle, the pandemic is now in the medium-term window (4-10 years), so individual sentence scores are capped in the mid-range; aggravated statements that tie directly to ongoing operational or financial strain receive scores of 5-6, while generic or mitigated references drop to 0-2.  Collectively, the evidence supports a moderate-to-elevated risk posture that KMB continues to monitor and disclose.

evidence_list.snippet: We face various risks related to health epidemics, pandemics and similar outbreaks, which may have material adverse effects on our business, financial position, results of operations and cash flows.

components.reason: Explicitly cites pandemics as a risk category for the company.
Uses strong severity language: 'material adverse effects'.
Generic phrasing without COVID-specific detail and four-year time lag.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Straightforward acknowledgement of pandemic risk with severe wording, but generic and partially time-diluted.

evidence_list.snippet: Our business and financial results may be negatively impacted by health epidemics, pandemics and similar outbreaks.

components.reason: States potential negative impact on business and financial results.
Mentions epidemics and pandemics explicitly.
Highly generic statement; no specifics or forward metrics.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: A boiler-plate warning worth only a low score due to lack of specificity.

evidence_list.snippet: The COVID-19 pandemic has had and could continue to have negative impacts on our business, including causing significant volatility in demand for our products, changes in consumer behavior and preference, disruptions in our manufacturing and supply chain operations, disruptions to our cost saving programs, limitations on our employees’ ability to work and travel, significant changes in the economic or political conditions in markets in which we operate and related currency and commodity volatility.

components.reason: Directly attributes multiple past and future impacts to COVID-19.
Lists several specific operational and financial impact vectors (demand, supply chain, labor).
Forward-looking phrase 'could continue' signals ongoing exposure.
Medium-term time decay adjustment.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Highly detailed enumeration of continuing pandemic impacts warrants the highest allowable mid-term score.

evidence_list.snippet: Despite our efforts to manage these impacts, their ultimate impact also depends on factors beyond our knowledge or control, including the duration and severity of any such outbreak and actions taken to contain its spread and mitigate its public health effects.

components.reason: Highlights uncertainty and uncontrollable external factors.
Implied risk of prolonged or severe outbreaks.
No quantitative detail; indirect reference creates moderation.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Acknowledges uncertainty, but absence of specificity keeps severity low.

evidence_list.snippet: These activities are subject to inherent risks such as natural disasters, power outages, fires or explosions, labor strikes or labor shortages, terrorism, epidemics, pandemics (including the COVID-19 pandemic), import restrictions, regional economic, business, environmental or political events (including the wars in Ukraine and Israel), governmental regulatory requirements or nongovernmental voluntary actions in response to global climate change or other concerns regarding the sustainability of our business, which could disrupt our supply chain and impair our ability to manufacture or sell our products.

components.reason: Explicitly lists pandemics, including COVID-19, among disruptive risks.
Links these events to concrete operational harm: supply-chain disruption and impaired manufacturing or sales.
Long catalogue of other risks dilutes pandemic specificity and invokes time decay.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Supply-chain impairment reference boosts severity, but long catch-all list tempers the score.

evidence_list.snippet: We have seen and may continue to see an increase in the number of such attacks, especially as we continue operating under a hybrid working model under which employees can work and access our technology infrastructure remotely.

components.reason: Notes elevated cyber risk linked to pandemic-driven remote work.
Indicates future exposure ('may continue to see').
Indirect connection to pandemic; primary risk is cyber rather than health.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Remote-work vulnerability is pandemic-related but secondary, so impact is modest.

evidence_list.snippet: COVID-19 - The macro business environment has experienced unprecedented volatility in recent years reflecting the effects of the global COVID-19 pandemic on supply and demand dynamics.

components.reason: Attributes unprecedented volatility in supply-demand dynamics directly to the pandemic.
Highlights macro-level instability.
Historical framing implies partial normalization over time.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Recognizes pandemic-driven volatility but positions it as an historical trend, yielding a moderate score.

evidence_list.snippet: We have seen stabilization in demand across all of  our business segments during 2022 and 2023, and we expect this trend to continue.

components.reason: Indicates mitigation: demand has stabilized post-pandemic.
Still implicitly references earlier pandemic volatility.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Positive stabilization entirely offsets residual risk, driving the snippet score to neutral.

evidence_list.snippet: The pandemic significantly disrupted supply chains across the globe, primarily due to the very significant fluctuations in demand and related transportation and labor supply issues.

components.reason: Specifies global supply-chain disruption caused by the pandemic.
Details mechanisms (demand swings, transport and labor issues).
References past disruption more than future; time decay applies.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Clear causal link to supply-chain risk, but phrased historically so impact is moderate.

evidence_list.snippet: Resulting supply shortages led to record levels of inflation in commodities and other costs.

components.reason: Connects pandemic-driven shortages to record cost inflation.
No forward-looking language; historical account only.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Shows severe past impact (record inflation) but lacks forward risk context.

evidence_list.snippet: During 2023, inflation slowed, but costs remain elevated across many categories of our raw materials, labor, energy and other input costs, as well as transportation costs, and we expect that these elevated levels could persist in 2024, although at a decreasing rate of inflation compared to the prior fiscal year.

components.reason: Acknowledges ongoing elevated cost levels tied to pandemic after-effects.
Projects persistence into 2024, confirming forward risk.
Partial mitigation (inflation slowing).

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Forward-looking cost pressure keeps risk moderate despite some easing.

evidence_list.snippet: Additionally, consumer purchasing power has generally been impacted negatively by the inflation driven by the effects of the pandemic which can impact consumer purchasing patterns.

components.reason: Links pandemic-driven inflation to reduced consumer purchasing power and demand risk.
No quantification; indirect effect and time decay.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Identifies demand-side risk but without depth or metrics, yielding a low score.
